calculators.title: Glasgow-Blatchford score

options.label: Not low: man 13 or more, woman 12 or more

bands.text: 0 or 1: very low risk; outpatient care can be considered
2 or more: not very low risk; admit

calculators.note: BUN and hemoglobin in US units (Scand J Trauma 2015); Blatchford's own cuts are urea 6.5, 8, 10 and 25 mmol/L and hemoglobin 130, 120 and 100 g/L in men, 120 and 100 in women (BMJ Open Gastroenterol 2018), whose systolic bands are used here. The International Consensus sends 1 or less home; NICE considers early discharge at 0.

nodes.ask: GI bleeding. First moves?
options: Two large-bore IVs, crossmatch, blood count and clotting; ask about antithrombotics and liver disease
Endoscopy first, before any fluids or blood, to find the source quickly
Hold fluids in a hypotensive patient until the first hemoglobin is back
Colloid boluses as the first fluid; labs once the pressure recovers
nodes.chainStep: Hemodynamics first; two large-bore IVs; blood count, crossmatch, electrolytes, coagulation; ask about anticoagulants, antiplatelets and liver disease
nodes.why: Resuscitation starts as soon as the patient is unstable, with crystalloid: colloids add cost without a survival benefit. Blood typing, hemoglobin, electrolytes and coagulation go off at once, and the history asks about antiplatelets, anticoagulants and liver disease, because each one changes the next step. Endoscopy comes once resuscitation is under way, never before it.

nodes.ask: On warfarin, INR 3.6, still bleeding. Reversal?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K, without delaying endoscopy
Fresh frozen plasma alone until the INR is below 1.5
IV vitamin K alone, then repeat the INR in 6 hours
Prothrombin complex concentrate, and delay endoscopy until the INR is normal
nodes.chainStep: Prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K for active bleeding; endoscopy is not delayed for the INR
nodes.why: Active bleeding on warfarin calls for prothrombin complex concentrate with vitamin K, the preferred combination for urgent reversal: PCC acts faster than plasma with little risk of fluid overload. Plasma is the fallback only when PCC is unavailable. Coagulopathy is treated as needed, but endoscopy is not delayed for the INR. The North American GI guideline is more cautious: it suggests against vitamin K and plasma and gives PCC only if needed.

orders.dose: Kcentra, for acute major bleeding: INR 2 to under 4, 25 units/kg (not over 2,500 units); INR 4 to 6, 35 units/kg (3,500); over 6, 50 units/kg (5,000); weight counted up to 100 kg

nodes.ask: On apixaban, vomiting blood, BP 84/50. Anticoagulant?
options: Stop apixaban; resuscitate and scope without waiting for the drug to clear
Idarucizumab 5 g IV
Wait until apixaban clears before endoscopy
Four-factor PCC, and hold endoscopy until it has run
nodes.chainStep: Stop apixaban; resuscitate and scope without waiting for the drug to clear
nodes.why: The anticoagulant is withheld while the bleed goes on, and endoscopy is not delayed for it: a DOAC's half-life is 8 to 12 hours and its effect should be gone 1 to 2 days after the last dose. The North American GI guideline suggests against both andexanet and PCC in GI bleeding, and andexanet left the US market in December 2025 after the FDA judged its thrombotic risk to outweigh its benefit; NICE still allows it for life-threatening GI bleeding in the UK. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not the factor Xa inhibitors.

nodes.ask: Aspirin and clopidogrel, a drug-eluting stent 4 months ago. Antiplatelets?
options: Continue aspirin; hold clopidogrel briefly and restart it with cardiology
Stop both until a repeat endoscopy shows the ulcer has healed
Platelet transfusion to reverse both drugs before endoscopy
Stop aspirin, which harms the mucosa, and keep clopidogrel alone
nodes.chainStep: Continue aspirin; hold clopidogrel briefly and restart it with cardiology (not off more than 5 days with a drug-eluting stent); no platelet transfusion
nodes.why: Stopping both risks stent thrombosis within days, so aspirin, which causes less rebleeding, continues, and clopidogrel is paused only briefly: with a drug-eluting stent it should not be off for more than 5 days. Low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention continues once hemostasis is achieved; clopidogrel is discussed with the cardiologist. Platelet transfusion has no benefit in a patient with a normal count.

nodes.ask: Red cell transfusion strategy?
options: Restrictive: transfuse below 7 to 8 g/dL, higher with heart disease; massive bleeding follows its protocol
Liberal: transfuse to keep the hemoglobin above 10 g/dL and protect the heart
No red cells until the hemoglobin is below 6 g/dL
Plasma and platelets routinely with the red cells to prevent a coagulopathy
nodes.chainStep: Restrictive red cells: transfuse below 7 to 8 g/dL (higher with heart disease); massive bleeding follows the massive transfusion protocol
nodes.why: A restrictive strategy lowers mortality and rebleeding. The International Consensus transfuses below 8 g/dL without cardiovascular disease and at a higher threshold with it; WSES keeps the hemoglobin above 7; Baveno VII targets 7 to 8 in variceal bleeding. In massive bleeding the hemoglobin lags behind the loss, so blood, platelets and clotting factors follow the local massive bleeding protocol and the clinical picture. Platelets and plasma are not routine.

nodes.ask: Upper GI bleed, stable. Risk score before deciding on admission?
options: Glasgow-Blatchford score
AIMS65 to select patients for discharge
The full Rockall score before endoscopy
No score; clinical judgment alone
nodes.chainStep: Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment; 0 or 1 is very low risk
nodes.why: The Glasgow-Blatchford score is the pre-endoscopy tool: it misclassifies 1% or fewer of high-risk patients as low risk. AIMS65 can miss about 20% of high-risk patients at low cut-offs, and the full Rockall score belongs after endoscopy. A score gives the consistency that clinical judgment cannot.

nodes.ask: Blatchford 0. Disposition?
options: Discharge with outpatient endoscopy
Admit for endoscopy within 12 hours
Admit for an IV PPI infusion and observation
CT angiography before discharge
nodes.chainStep: Blatchford 0 or 1: discharge with outpatient endoscopy
nodes.why: A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 or 1 marks very low risk of rebleeding or death: no admission and no inpatient endoscopy, with endoscopy as an outpatient. NICE considers early discharge at a score of 0. Urgent endoscopy within 12 hours is for the high-risk group, and CT is for when endoscopy is not available.

nodes.ask: Admitted, Blatchford 2 or more, stable after fluids. Endoscopy when?
options: Within 24 hours of presentation (WSES: within 12 in its high-risk group)
Only if the hemoglobin keeps falling on serial checks
Elective, as an outpatient after discharge
CT angiography first; endoscopy only if it is positive
nodes.chainStep: Upper endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation (within 12 hours in the WSES high-risk group)
nodes.why: Admitted patients get endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation. WSES asks for 12 hours in its high-risk group; the International Consensus could not recommend for or against 12 hours. Endoscopy diagnoses, treats and grades the risk of rebleeding, so a steady hemoglobin is no reason to skip it. Angiography before endoscopy gives unacceptable rates of negative studies, and CT is for when endoscopy is not available.

nodes.ask: High-risk stigmata on the ulcer. Endoscopic treatment?
options: Hemostasis with clips or thermal coagulation, usually combined with epinephrine injection
Epinephrine injection alone, repeated until the bleeding stops
Hemostatic powder sprayed on the ulcer as the only treatment
No endoscopic treatment; a high-dose PPI infusion alone
nodes.chainStep: Endoscopic hemostasis: clips or thermal coagulation, usually with epinephrine; never epinephrine alone
nodes.why: Spurting, oozing and visible-vessel ulcers get endoscopic hemostasis. Clips, thermocoagulation or sclerosant all work, and WSES prefers two modalities. Epinephrine alone is not enough: clips beat it for rebleeding, and NICE rules it out as monotherapy. Hemostatic powder is a temporizing measure, not the sole treatment, and drugs alone rebleed more than endoscopic therapy.

nodes.ask: Fresh melena after endoscopic treatment; ulcer under 2 cm; pressure holding. Next?
options: Repeat endoscopy with further endoscopic treatment
Emergency surgery
Increase the PPI infusion and observe
Transfuse to a hemoglobin of 10 and observe
nodes.chainStep: Repeat endoscopy with further endoscopic treatment for a stable rebleed
nodes.why: Endoscopy is the first-line treatment for a rebleeding ulcer, at the earliest opportunity. In the randomized trial, endoscopic retreatment gave lasting control in 35 of 48 patients with fewer complications than surgery; hypotension and an ulcer of 2 cm or more predicted its failure.

nodes.ask: Two endoscopic treatments have failed; still bleeding. Next?
options: Angiographic embolization where available; surgery if it is not, or if it fails
A third endoscopic attempt with clips and thermal therapy
Hemostatic powder spray as the definitive treatment
Transfuse and continue the high-dose PPI infusion, then reassess
nodes.chainStep: Angiographic embolization after two failed endoscopic treatments; surgery if it is unavailable or fails
nodes.why: When endoscopic hemostasis fails twice in a stable patient, WSES suggests angioembolization where the skills and equipment exist, and surgical hemostasis when it is not available. ACR rates visceral arteriography usually appropriate for bleeding that continues after endoscopic treatment; NICE offers patients who rebleed a repeat endoscopy with further treatment or emergency surgery. Powder only temporizes.

nodes.ask: Clean-based ulcer, no stigmata of bleeding. Next?
options: No endoscopic hemostasis; an H. pylori test and early discharge
Clips and epinephrine on the ulcer base to prevent rebleeding
High-dose IV PPI infusion for 72 hours
CT angiography to look for a second source
nodes.chainStep: Clean-based ulcer: no endoscopic hemostasis; H. pylori test; early discharge
nodes.why: Endoscopic hemostasis is for spurting, oozing and visible-vessel ulcers; a clean base needs none, and endoscopy is what identifies the low-risk patient for early discharge. Every bleeding ulcer gets an H. pylori test. The 72-hour high-dose infusion is for high-risk stigmata after endoscopic therapy.

nodes.ask: Melena, upper endoscopy normal, stable. Next?
options: Colonoscopy; then the small bowel (CT enterography or capsule) if both are negative
Push enteroscopy before a colonoscopy
Exploratory laparotomy to find the source
Empiric PPI for 8 weeks and no further tests
nodes.chainStep: Normal upper endoscopy: colonoscopy next; CT enterography or capsule endoscopy if both are negative
nodes.why: Melena can come from the lower tract. When an adequate colonoscopy and upper endoscopy are both negative, the small bowel is the usual source, and capsule endoscopy and CT enterography are usually appropriate. Surgery is not a tool to localize bleeding in a stable patient.

nodes.ask: Hematemesis, BP 84/50 after 1 L of crystalloid. Next?
options: Blood under the massive transfusion protocol, then endoscopy as soon as resuscitated
Wait for the hemoglobin before giving any blood
Endoscopy within 24 hours, as for a stable bleed
Endoscopy now, before any resuscitation, to stop the source
nodes.chainStep: Blood under the massive transfusion protocol; endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
nodes.why: In shock the hemoglobin lags behind the loss, so transfusion follows the clinical picture and the massive bleeding protocol, not the number. Unstable patients with severe upper bleeding get endoscopy immediately after resuscitation and stabilization, and in an actively bleeding ulcer endoscopy is part of the resuscitation.

nodes.ask: Cirrhosis with an upper GI bleed. Before endoscopy?
options: Vasoactive drug and antibiotic prophylaxis now, before endoscopy
Wait for endoscopy to confirm varices before any drug
Fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR before endoscopy
Tranexamic acid infusion to stabilize the clot
nodes.chainStep: Octreotide 50 micrograms IV, then 25 to 50 micrograms per hour (or terlipressin 2 mg IV every 4 hours), and antibiotic prophylaxis from admission, before endoscopy; restrictive transfusion to 7 to 8 g/dL
nodes.why: In suspected variceal bleeding a vasoactive drug (terlipressin, somatostatin or octreotide) starts as soon as possible and runs for 2 to 5 days, and antibiotic prophylaxis is part of the treatment from admission. Plasma does not correct the coagulopathy of cirrhosis and can worsen portal hypertension; tranexamic acid and factor VIIa are not recommended.

options: Within 12 hours of presentation, once resuscitated; sooner if unstable
Only if bleeding continues after 48 hours of drugs
After 5 days of vasoactive therapy
Within 72 hours, once the INR has been corrected

nodes.why: Baveno VII sets endoscopy within 12 hours of presentation after resuscitation, and as soon as safely possible in an unstable patient; NICE and BSG 2015 set 24 hours, earlier with heavy bleeding, so 12 hours meets both. Sclerotherapy
Cyanoacrylate glue injection
Hemostatic powder alone

nodes.why: Ligation is the recommended endoscopic therapy for bleeding esophageal varices. Tissue adhesive is for isolated gastric varices and those extending beyond the cardia, and hemostatic powder is not first-line therapy for variceal bleeding.

options: Pre-emptive covered TIPS within 72 hours, ideally within 24
Covered TIPS only if he rebleeds after discharge
Balloon tamponade for 24 hours, then decide

nodes.chainStep: Pre-emptive covered TIPS within 72 hours (ideally under 24) for Child-Pugh C under 14, or B over 7 with active bleeding at endoscopy
nodes.why: Child-Pugh C under 14, or B over 7 with active bleeding at the first endoscopy, meets the criteria for pre-emptive PTFE-covered TIPS within 72 hours, ideally under 24. In the trial behind it, treatment failure fell from 50% to 3%. Balloon tamponade is a bridge for bleeding that will not stop, and TIPS after a rebleed is for patients who rebleed despite a beta blocker and ligation.

options: Vasoactive drug 2 to 5 days, then a beta blocker or carvedilol plus repeat banding
Pre-emptive covered TIPS within 72 hours, before discharge
A beta blocker alone, with no further ligation sessions
Repeat ligation alone; a beta blocker only after a second bleed
nodes.chainStep: Vasoactive drug for 2 to 5 days; then a non-selective beta blocker or carvedilol plus repeat band ligation
nodes.why: The vasoactive drug runs 2 to 5 days. First-line prevention of a rebleed combines a traditional non-selective beta blocker (propranolol or nadolol) or carvedilol with band ligation; either alone is for patients who cannot have the other. She does not meet the pre-emptive TIPS criteria, and TIPS is the choice for those who rebleed despite the combination.

Fresh frozen plasma and platelets to correct the clotting first
Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours, once the bleeding settles
Tranexamic acid infusion and a third banding session

nodes.why: Bleeding that defeats combined drug and endoscopic therapy is best managed by salvage PTFE-covered TIPS; balloon tamponade or a self-expanding metal stent bridges to it, and the stent works as well and is safer. Variceal bleeding is driven by portal pressure, not the clotting tests, so plasma does not help, and tranexamic acid is not recommended.

nodes.why: Tissue adhesive is the recommended endoscopic therapy for isolated gastric varices and for gastro-oesophageal varices that extend beyond the cardia; ligation or adhesive can be used for the type that continues from the esophagus (type 1). TIPS follows when the glue does not control the bleeding.

Mesenteric angiography first

nodes.why: In a stable patient colonoscopy finds and treats the source, and urgent colonoscopy has not beaten a planned one. CT angiography is also usually appropriate while bleeding is active. Embolization needs a bleeding point seen at angiography, and surgery is not used to find the source in a stable patient.

Capsule endoscopy before any upper endoscopy

Repeat the same colonoscopy tomorrow

nodes.why: Up to 15% of suspected lower bleeds have an upper source, so upper endoscopy follows an adequate negative colonoscopy; only a suboptimal study is repeated first. If both are normal, the small bowel is next, by capsule endoscopy or CT enterography.

Subtotal colectomy now, without localizing the source
nodes.chainStep: CT angiography now (upper endoscopy first if an upper source is likely); catheter angiography and embolization of any bleeding point
nodes.why: CT angiography is feasible even in an unstable patient and locates the bleeding for targeted embolization or surgery; a red cell scan takes an hour or more and has no role here. Colonoscopy needs a rapid preparation, which limits it when unstable, and surgery without localization is kept for bleeding that cannot be controlled. A brisk upper bleed can also present as hematochezia.

outcomes.if: Colonic bleeding point; contrast extravasation in the colon
Upper source; extravasation in the duodenum
No extravasation; now stable after blood

orders.item: Catheter angiography after a negative CT
orders.dose: Avoid in a stable patient; conservative management can start

outcomes.if: No extravasation, still unstable; case by case

nodes.ask: CT angiography: active extravasation in the sigmoid colon. Next?
options: Catheter angiography and embolization as soon as possible
Repeat CT angiography in 6 hours
Tagged red cell scan to confirm
Colonoscopy after bowel preparation tomorrow
nodes.chainStep: Catheter angiography and embolization as soon as possible after a positive CT angiogram
nodes.why: Lower bleeding is intermittent, so arteriography follows a positive CT as soon as possible, and embolization follows at once when extravasation is seen. Major ischemia after embolization is uncommon, about 3% or less, and stopping the bleed buys time to stabilize and prepare the bowel if surgery is needed.

sources.where: Variant 1, F (transcatheter arteriography); Special treatment considerations, transcatheter embolization; Variant 2, E (surgery); Variant 2 rating table; Variant 2, D (RBC scan)

nodes.ask: CT angiography: contrast pooling in the duodenum. Next?
options: Upper endoscopy now, to treat the source
Colonoscopy after bowel preparation
Repeat CT angiography in 6 hours
Catheter angiography of the gastroduodenal artery first
nodes.chainStep: Upper endoscopy now for a duodenal source on CT angiography
nodes.why: A minority of upper bleeds present with hematochezia. Once the CT points to the duodenum, endoscopy is the usual first test and treatment for an upper source, and angiography is second line.

nodes.summary: Very low-risk upper bleed (Blatchford 0 or 1): home, with an outpatient endoscopy.

Bleeding ulcer with high-risk stigmata: endoscopic hemostasis, a high-dose PPI for 72 hours, oral PPI for 6 to 8 weeks, H. pylori testing and treatment, and low-dose aspirin, when taken for secondary prevention, continued once hemostasis is secure.

Unstable rebleed after endoscopic treatment: NICE offers interventional radiology, with urgent surgery if it is not promptly available; WSES operates without another endoscopy. Not walked further in this version.
Negative CT angiography in a patient who stays unstable: managed case by case (ACR). Not walked further in this version.
Mallory-Weiss tear: not walked further in this version.
Ulcer still bleeding after two endoscopic treatments: angiographic embolization, or surgery when it is unavailable or fails.
Ulcer with an adherent clot: the sources allow endoscopic therapy or a PPI alone, and WSES irrigates rather than pulls the clot off. The choice between them is not walked further in this version.
Clean-based ulcer: no endoscopic therapy, H. pylori testing, early discharge. The PPI regimen for a clean base is not yet in this pathway.
Melena with a normal upper endoscopy: colonoscopy, then the small bowel.
High-risk variceal bleed: vasoactive drug, antibiotics, band ligation and pre-emptive covered TIPS within 72 hours.
Controlled esophageal variceal bleed: vasoactive drug for 2 to 5 days, antibiotics, then a beta blocker or carvedilol plus repeat ligation.
Refractory variceal bleed: balloon tamponade or a stent as a bridge to salvage covered TIPS.
Gastric variceal bleed: cyanoacrylate injection, TIPS if it fails.
Minor lower bleed that has stopped: no urgent intervention, colonoscopy arranged electively. The Oakland discharge threshold is not yet in this pathway.
Diverticular bleed found and treated at colonoscopy.
No colonic source: upper endoscopy, then the small bowel.
Unstable lower bleed: CT angiography, then embolization of the bleeding point.

cases.label: Very low-risk upper bleed
cases.vignette: 34-year-old man who vomited a small amount of coffee-ground material once after a night of retching. No melena, no fainting, no heart failure or liver disease. BP 132/80, HR 78.

results.meds: No regular medicines; no NSAIDs, antiplatelets or anticoagulants.
results.first_look: Stable; brown stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 0.

cases.label: Ulcer bleed on dual antiplatelets
cases.vignette: 66-year-old man with a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 4 months ago, 2 days of black stools. No fainting, no heart failure. BP 124/76, HR 92.

results.meds: Aspirin and clopidogrel daily since the stent.
results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, BUN 21 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 4.
results.egd_result: A 1 cm duodenal ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel.
results.rebleed_check: No further bleeding over 72 hours; hemoglobin steady at 11.8 g/dL.

cases.label: Ulcer that rebleeds once
cases.vignette: 58-year-old woman taking naproxen for knee pain, black stools since yesterday. No fainting. BP 118/72, HR 96.

results.meds: Naproxen twice daily; no antiplatelets or anticoagulants.
results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, BUN 30 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 6.
results.rebleed_check: Day 2: fresh melena, HR 104, BP 118/70. The ulcer measured 1 cm.
results.repeat_result: Repeat endoscopy: clips and thermal therapy; no further bleeding.

cases.label: Ulcer that fails two endoscopic treatments
cases.vignette: 71-year-old man on low-dose aspirin since a myocardial infarction, a day of black stools. No fainting, no heart failure or liver disease. BP 122/74, HR 98.

results.meds: Aspirin 81 mg daily for secondary prevention; no other antithrombotic drug.
results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, BUN 26 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 7.
results.egd_result: A 1.5 cm duodenal bulb ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel.
results.rebleed_check: Day 1: fresh melena, BP 116/70, HR 102. The ulcer measured 1.5 cm.
results.repeat_result: Retreated with clips; 6 hours later fresh melena again, hemoglobin down 2 g/dL, BP 110/68.

cases.label: Clean-based ulcer
cases.vignette: 62-year-old man on rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation, 2 days of black stools after a week of ibuprofen for back pain. No fainting, no heart failure. BP 128/80, HR 88.

results.meds: Rivaroxaban daily, last dose last night; ibuprofen for a week. No vomiting of blood; vital signs steady.
results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, BUN 19 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 4.
results.egd_result: A 7 mm clean-based duodenal ulcer; no stigmata of recent bleeding.

cases.label: Ulcer with an adherent clot
cases.vignette: 55-year-old woman, a day of black stools after two weeks of diclofenac for a sprained ankle. No fainting, no heart failure. BP 120/76, HR 94.

results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, BUN 23 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 5.
results.egd_result: A 1 cm gastric ulcer covered by an adherent clot that stays on gentle irrigation; no active bleeding.

cases.label: Melena with a normal upper endoscopy
cases.vignette: 77-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, with aortic stenosis, 2 days of black tarry stools and fatigue; none since last night. No fainting, no heart failure. BP 126/70, HR 90.

results.meds: Warfarin; INR 2.4. No melena or hematemesis since last night.
results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, BUN 20 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 4.
results.egd_result: Normal to the second part of the duodenum; no blood in the stomach.

cases.label: Ulcer bleed on warfarin
cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, vomiting fresh blood and passing black stools since this morning. No fainting, no heart failure. BP 112/70, HR 96. Weight 70 kg.

results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, BUN 25 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 5.
results.egd_result: A 1 cm gastric ulcer with a spurting vessel.

cases.label: Upper bleed in shock on apixaban
cases.vignette: 69-year-old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation, vomiting large amounts of bright red blood, pale and clammy. BP 84/50, HR 124.

results.meds: Apixaban twice daily, last dose this morning.

results.egd_result: After resuscitation: a 1.5 cm duodenal ulcer, spurting.

cases.label: Variceal bleed, Child-Pugh C

results.tips_risk: Child-Pugh C, 11 points; bleeding actively at endoscopy, stopped by ligation.

cases.label: Variceal bleed, Child-Pugh B

results.varix_result: Large esophageal varices, not actively bleeding, with blood in the stomach and no other source.
results.tips_risk: Child-Pugh B, 8 points; no active bleeding at endoscopy; varices banded.

cases.label: Variceal bleed that will not stop
cases.vignette: 48-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis, massive hematemesis, intubated to protect his airway. BP 90/54, HR 118.

results.first_look: Known cirrhosis; jaundice and ascites; BP 92/56 after blood.
results.tips_risk: Still bleeding despite octreotide and two rounds of banding.

cases.label: Gastric variceal bleed
cases.vignette: 57-year-old woman with cirrhosis, vomiting blood and passing black stools. BP 112/68, HR 102.

results.first_look: Known cirrhosis; ascites; stable after fluids.
results.varix_result: A large isolated gastric varix in the fundus with fresh clot; no esophageal varices.

cases.label: Cirrhosis, but the bleed is an ulcer
cases.vignette: 63-year-old man with known cirrhosis who takes ibuprofen for gout, vomiting coffee-ground material and passing black stools. BP 116/70, HR 98.

results.first_look: Ascites and spider angiomas; stable after fluids.
results.varix_result: Small esophageal varices without stigmata; a 1 cm duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel.

cases.label: Large ulcer that rebleeds into shock
cases.vignette: 64-year-old man taking ibuprofen for back pain, 2 days of black stools. No fainting, no heart failure or liver disease. BP 120/78, HR 96.

results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; black stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, BUN 24 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 7.
results.egd_result: A 2.5 cm posterior duodenal ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel.

cases.label: Mallory-Weiss tear
cases.vignette: 28-year-old man who vomited bright red blood after retching through the night. No melena, no fainting, no heart failure or liver disease. BP 118/72, HR 104.

results.first_look: Stable after 1 L of crystalloid; brown stool on rectal exam; no stigmata of liver disease.
results.gbs_result: Hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL, BUN 19 mg/dL. Glasgow-Blatchford score 3.

cases.label: Minor lower bleed that has stopped
cases.vignette: 64-year-old man, one episode of bright red blood mixed with stool this morning, none since. No abdominal pain. BP 128/78, HR 76.

results.first_look: Stable; a little red blood on rectal exam.
results.lower_sev: Hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL; no further bleeding in the department.

cases.label: Diverticular bleed, stable

results.first_look: Stable after fluids; maroon blood on rectal exam.

cases.label: Normal colonoscopy
cases.vignette: 70-year-old woman, two large painless dark red stools overnight. BP 124/76, HR 90.

results.first_look: Stable after fluids; dark red blood on rectal exam.
